title: Questions at an izakaya
summary: Use question words to establish time, place, people, quantities, and preferences during a restaurant exchange.
takeaways: Question words stay in the normal sentence slot.
どちら compares two choices; どの must modify a noun.
Counters change shape, so learn them as answer patterns rather than isolated vocabulary.

grammar.title: Leave the unknown in place
grammar.pattern: Noun は Question word ですか
grammar.summary: Japanese does not move the question word to the front. Put いつ, どこ, だれ, or [[何時|なんじ]] where the missing information belongs.

examples.note: Here, どちら politely asks about origin; it is not a two-choice question.

grammar.title: Compare two choices
grammar.pattern: A と B と どちらが …
grammar.summary: Use どちら for a polite choice between two things. The chosen thing is commonly marked by が with preference adjectives.

examples.english: Which do you like, sushi or tempura?
Which would you prefer, table seating or tatami seating?

grammar.title: Choose one item from a category
grammar.summary: Use どの before a noun when you are choosing one item from a known category. It means “which + noun,” as in どの色 (which color) or どの席 (which seat).
grammar.caution: どの cannot stand alone: use どれ for “which one?” Compare どの色がいいですか (Which color?) with どれがいいですか (Which one?).

grammar.title: Offer a quantity
grammar.pattern: Noun を いくつ お持ちしましょうか
grammar.summary: Use いくつ to ask for an unspecified number of countable items. In service language, お持ちしましょうか politely offers to bring them.

examples.english: How many beers shall I bring you?
examples.note: A server can use this to confirm the quantity before bringing the order.

recall.prompt: Can どの stand by itself?
recall.answer: No. It must modify a noun.

recall.prompt: Where does a Japanese question word go?
recall.answer: In the same sentence position as the missing answer.
